title: Modern BCI companies, speech neuroprostheses, and ethics
text:
14_03  SPEECH NEUROPROSTHESES, THE BCI INDUSTRY, AND ETHICS

By the early 2020s, brain-computer interfaces crossed two thresholds at once. Scientifically, decoders built on deep learning and language models began to restore communication at rates approaching natural conversation. Commercially, several well-funded companies began human trials of implantable systems designed for daily use outside the laboratory. Both developments raise questions that are not only technical: who owns neural data, what happens when a company that maintains your implant goes bankrupt, and what should "mental privacy" mean? This section covers the speech results, the main engineering approaches in industry, and the ethical issues, keeping to what has been published.

SPEECH NEUROPROSTHESES

Speech is the richest human output channel, at around 150 words per minute in conversation. Its loss, through brainstem stroke, ALS or other conditions, is devastating. Decoding attempted speech from cortex became a major goal.

Electrocorticography (ECoG), grids of electrodes placed on the surface of cortex, had been used for years in epilepsy patients being monitored before surgery. Edward Chang's group at the University of California, San Francisco used such recordings to map how ventral sensorimotor cortex represents articulators such as lips, tongue, jaw and larynx. In 2019 Gopala Anumanchipalli, Josh Chartier and Chang reported in Nature that speech could be synthesised from cortical activity in people who could speak, by decoding articulatory movements first and then converting them to sound, an intermediate representation that improved performance.

In 2021 David Moses, Chang and colleagues reported in the New England Journal of Medicine that a man who had lost the ability to speak after a brainstem stroke more than 15 years earlier could produce sentences from a 50-word vocabulary through an implanted ECoG array, decoding at about 15 words per minute with a language model helping to correct errors.

In August 2023 Nature published two papers together.

Francis Willett, Erin Kunz, Chaofei Fan, Jaimie Henderson, Krishna Shenoy and colleagues (Shenoy died in 2023 before publication) reported a speech BCI using four Utah arrays implanted in a participant with ALS who could no longer speak intelligibly. Arrays in ventral premotor cortex (area 6v) carried information about attempted speech. An RNN decoded phoneme probabilities every 80 ms, and a language model assembled words. Communication reached about 62 words per minute, with a word error rate of about 9 percent on a 50-word vocabulary and about 24 percent on a 125,000-word vocabulary.

Sean Metzger, Kaylo Littlejohn, Alexander Silva, David Moses, Chang and colleagues reported a high-density ECoG system with 253 electrodes in a woman with severe paralysis after a brainstem stroke. It decoded text at a median of about 78 words per minute, synthesised speech personalised with a recording of her voice from before her injury, and animated a digital avatar's facial movements.

In 2024 Nicholas Card, Maitreyee Wairagkar, David Brandman, Sergey Stavisky and colleagues at the University of California, Davis reported in the New England Journal of Medicine that a man with ALS, implanted with four microelectrode arrays, achieved about 97.5 percent word accuracy with a large vocabulary over months of use, including at home in conversation. In 2025 Wairagkar and colleagues reported in Nature a system synthesising voice almost instantaneously from neural activity, allowing the participant to modulate intonation and produce sounds beyond a fixed vocabulary.

These systems share a structure that will be familiar from 14_02 and from automatic speech recognition: neural features in short bins, a recurrent or transformer network producing phoneme or articulatory probabilities, connectionist temporal classification or similar alignment-free training objectives, and a language model as a prior. The neuroscience contributes the right recording location and an understanding of what the signals represent; the machine learning contributes the decoder and the prior.

RESTORING MOVEMENT THROUGH THE SPINE

BCIs can also reconnect brain to body. Henri Lorach, Gregoire Courtine, Jocelyne Bloch and colleagues reported in Nature in 2023 a "brain-spine interface" in which ECoG-like implants over motor cortex decoded walking intentions and drove epidural electrical stimulation of the lumbar spinal cord, allowing a man with chronic spinal cord injury to stand and walk more naturally, including on stairs and uneven ground. Notably, he regained some walking ability even when the system was turned off, after neurorehabilitation, suggesting that the system promoted recovery of spared connections.

ENGINEERING APPROACHES IN INDUSTRY

Commercial efforts differ mainly in where and how they record, trading invasiveness against signal quality. The descriptions below summarise publicly reported designs; details and trial status change quickly, and the companies' own claims should be distinguished from peer-reviewed results.

Penetrating microelectrode arrays. Blackrock Neurotech supplies the Utah array used in most academic intracortical studies. Paradromics has developed a high-channel-count implant designed for fully implanted, wireless data transmission.

Flexible thread electrodes with robotic insertion. Neuralink, founded in 2016, uses many thin polymer threads carrying electrodes, inserted into cortex by a surgical robot to avoid blood vessels, with a sealed, wireless implant in the skull that charges inductively. The company announced its first human implant in January 2024, in a participant with quadriplegia who used it to control a computer cursor and play games. The company later reported that a number of threads had retracted from the brain in that participant, reducing the number of effective electrodes, and that it compensated with changes to the recording and decoding software. Much of the information about this system has come from company presentations rather than peer-reviewed papers, which is a common concern raised by academic researchers about the BCI industry.

Endovascular electrodes. Synchron's Stentrode is a stent-mounted electrode array delivered through the jugular vein into a large vein (the superior sagittal sinus) lying next to motor cortex, avoiding open-brain surgery. Signals are lower in resolution than penetrating electrodes, but participants with paralysis have used it to control digital devices for tasks such as messaging, with early feasibility studies in Australia and the United States.

Thin-film surface arrays. Precision Neuroscience, founded by former Neuralink co-founder Benjamin Rapoport and others, develops thin, flexible arrays with many electrodes placed on the cortical surface through a narrow slit in the skull, aiming for minimal invasiveness while recording at high density.

Non-invasive approaches continue as well, using EEG, functional near-infrared spectroscopy, and magnetoencephalography with new optically pumped magnetometers. Researchers have also reported decoding semantic content from fMRI with language models (Jerry Tang, Alexander Huth and colleagues, Nature Neuroscience, 2023), though this required many hours of training data per person in a scanner and the cooperation of the participant; the authors showed that decoding failed when participants resisted, and discussed privacy implications.

ENGINEERING CHALLENGES

For a mechatronics student, the open problems are concrete:

Biocompatibility and longevity. The brain reacts to implants with inflammation and glial encapsulation. Mechanical mismatch between stiff electrodes and soft brain tissue, which moves with pulse and respiration, is thought to contribute. Flexible materials, smaller cross-sections and coatings are active research areas.

Power and heat. A wireless implant must amplify, digitise and transmit data from hundreds or thousands of channels within strict limits on tissue heating (on the order of 1 to 2 degrees Celsius is a commonly cited safety ceiling). This forces on-implant data reduction, for example transmitting only threshold crossings or band power rather than raw voltages, and low-power ASIC design.

Bandwidth. Raw data from 1,000 channels at 30 kHz and 10-12 bits is several hundred megabits per second, far beyond practical low-power wireless links, so compression and on-chip feature extraction are essential; this is an area where neuromorphic ideas (13_04) are relevant.

Hermetic packaging, surgical workflow, MRI compatibility, cybersecurity of wireless links, and long-term support all matter as much as decoding accuracy.

ETHICS

Neurotechnology raises distinctive ethical questions.

Abandonment. When a company supporting an implant fails, patients may be left with unsupported devices. IEEE Spectrum reported in 2022 that people with Second Sight's Argus II retinal implant were left without support for their devices after the company's financial troubles. This case is now widely cited in discussions of obligations to trial participants and users, including ongoing maintenance, explantation options and data access.

Informed consent and vulnerability. Participants are often people with severe paralysis or locked-in syndrome, for whom communication itself may be limited and hopes high. Consent processes must manage expectations about benefit, risks of surgery, and what happens at the end of a trial.

Neural data privacy. Neural data may reveal health information, emotional states, or intentions. In 2021 Chile amended its constitution to protect mental integrity and brain activity in the context of neurotechnology, and in 2024 the US state of Colorado amended its privacy law to treat neural data as sensitive data. Scholars such as Rafael Yuste, who has campaigned for "neurorights", and legal scholars such as Nita Farahany have argued for new protections, while others argue existing human rights frameworks can be extended.

Agency and identity. Closed-loop systems that stimulate, such as deep brain stimulation for Parkinson's disease, have occasionally been associated with changes in mood or behaviour in some patients, raising questions about responsibility for actions influenced by a device. When an AI-assisted speech BCI autocompletes a sentence, whose words are they? Designers increasingly include confirmation steps and ways for users to correct or veto output.

Equity. Implants are expensive and require specialised surgery and support; who gets access is an ethical question as much as a medical one.

CONNECTIONS TO AI AND MACHINE LEARNING

1. Language models as priors. Speech BCIs combine noisy neural decoders with language models, sometimes large ones. This improves accuracy but introduces a risk: a strong prior can produce fluent text the user did not intend. Measuring and controlling this, with confidence displays and user confirmation, is a human-AI alignment problem in miniature: making sure the system says what the person means.

2. Personalised generative models. Voice cloning from pre-injury recordings and avatar animation are applications of generative AI to restore identity, not just function.

3. Edge AI. Wireless implants push toward on-device inference with tight power budgets, the same constraints as edge and embedded ML, motivating quantised, sparse and spiking networks.

4. Foundation models for neural data. As more participants and sessions are recorded, models pretrained across people may reduce calibration time for each new user, as pretrained speech models did for speech recognition.

5. Data governance. The debate about neural data rights parallels debates about training data for AI: consent, ownership and secondary use. Neural data is unusually personal, so the stakes are higher.

SUMMARY

Speech neuroprostheses reported between 2021 and 2025 moved from a 50-word vocabulary at about 15 words per minute to large-vocabulary communication at tens of words per minute and near-instant voice synthesis, combining intracortical or ECoG recordings with deep learning and language models. Companies are pursuing penetrating, thread-based, endovascular and surface approaches, each trading invasiveness against signal quality, with peer-reviewed evidence still limited for some. Ethical issues include device abandonment, consent, neural data privacy, agency, and equity. The field is now as much an AI engineering discipline as a neuroscience one.
